content:
Rapper Macklemore has criticised after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's stadium tour for his pro-Palestinian remarks, with critics questioning why Kanye West—known for antisemitic statements—is still allowed to perform.

Twitch streamer Caroline Kwan wrote on X that the situation was "utterly absurd," pointing out that West (now known as Ye) released a song titled "Heil Hitler" just last year.

On Monday, Macklemore accused New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft of "mobilising" other venue owners to issue Sheeran an ultimatum: if Macklemore remained as the opening act, the eight shows on the tour would be cancelled.

Macklemore used his first two scheduled performances to chant "Free Palestine," and in one of his speeches expressed solidarity with the people of Gaza and the West Bank under Israeli occupation.

At another show, he told Jewish fans: "Criticising Israel, criticising apartheid, opposing genocide—that absolutely does not equate to criticising you. My message is peace: I hope all human beings can be treated with dignity, respect and equality."

Tour organisers told Rolling Stone on Monday that venues had warned them that if Macklemore stayed on the tour lineup, the venues would pull their bookings. Sheeran echoed those remarks on Tuesday.

Kraft, who is Jewish and a frequent supporter of pro-Israel causes, confirmed in his own statement that Macklemore would no longer be performing at Gillette Stadium, but did not respond to allegations that he had pressured other venues to follow suit.

The decision to drop the Seattle rapper from the tour has drawn the ire of some commentators, who noted that Ye performed two shows at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, this June—a venue reportedly among those opposing Macklemore's appearance.

In a column titled "The Absurd Hypocrisy Behind Dropping Macklemore," MS NOW columnist Noor Norman wrote that "the so-called anti-cancel-culture crowd is not only silent on the decision regarding Macklemore," but Ye "continues to tour at the same time."

The Atlantic's Jemele Hill wrote on X: "Someone who releases a song called 'Heil Hitler' and calls himself a Nazi can sell out stadiums. Say 'Free Palestine,' and you can't."

Although some overseas dates on Ye's tour have been cancelled over his past antisemitic remarks and security concerns, as of Tuesday all of his US concerts were going ahead as scheduled.

The hip-hop star's contract may explain part of the reason. His Tampa concert was announced only after years of public expressions of admiration for Hitler, and the announcement drew fierce bipartisan opposition in Florida calling for the show to be scrapped.

However, Ye reportedly inserted a clause in his contract barring the Tampa venue from cancelling the performance over his past comments. The rapper had earlier taken out a full-page ad in The Wall Street Journal apologising for his antisemitic remarks, claiming he had become "out of touch with reality" during a battle with bipolar disorder.

Because the stadium is publicly owned and operated, the possibility of cancellation also raised First Amendment concerns at the time—though those concerns reportedly did not stop the venue from joining the boycott against Macklemore.

It remains unclear whether AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas—where Ye is scheduled to perform in November and which is owned by the City of Arlington—has a similar contract with Ye.

HuffPost has reached out to representatives of both stadiums.
